entities.name: The Shepherd of Hermas
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Shepherd of Hermas, a Christian literary work believed to have been composed in the 1st or 2nd century CE, serves as a crucial artifact in understanding early Christian thought and community structure. Traditionally attributed to Hermas, a former slave turned Christian prophet, this text originated in the Roman Empire, likely in or around the city of Rome, and is notable for its allegorical visions and moral exhortations directed at the Christian community. Its significance lies in its unique blend of doctrine and ethics, offering a rare glimpse into the struggles and aspirations of early Christians amid a diverse and often hostile environment.

The work comprises five visions, twelve mandates, and ten similitudes, which collectively address themes of sin, repentance, and the nature of the Church. Notable for its emphasis on the importance of moral integrity and the necessity of repentance, the text reflects the burgeoning Christian community's values during a time when they were grappling with external pressures and internal divisions. The Shepherd of Hermas was widely read and respected in the early Church, influencing theological debates and pastoral practices before its eventual exclusion from the New Testament canon.

The legacy of The Shepherd of Hermas extends beyond its immediate historical context, impacting various theological discourses throughout the centuries. Its teachings on repentance and moral living resonate in later Christian writings and church teachings. The text was preserved through various manuscript traditions, influencing notable figures such as Tertullian and Origen, who recognized its pastoral value. The Shepherd's exploration of the relationship between faith and works has continued to spark discussion within Christian theology, especially during periods of reform and revival.

Their legacy is studied through the lens of historical causation.", "summary": "The Shepherd of Hermas (Greek: Ποιμήν τοῦ Ἑρμᾶ, Poimēn tou Herma) is an early Christian literary work composed c. 100–160 CE, attributed to a man named Hermas (possibly the brother of Pope Pius I), and one of the most widely read texts in the early Christian Church — included in some early canonical lists (notably the Codex Sinaiticus, where it follows the Apocalypse of John) and considered authoritative scripture by Clement of Alexandria, Origen, and Athanasius. The Shepherd of Hermas is structured as an apocalyptic vision in three sections: the Visions (five visions in which Hermas receives revelations from an elderly woman representing the Church and from the Shepherd, an angel of repentance); the Mandates (twelve commandments given by the Shepherd); and the Similitudes (ten parables explaining the mandates through allegorical imagery).

The Shepherd of Hermas is historically significant as the most important early Christian document addressing the question of post-baptismal sin — whether Christians who sin after baptism can be forgiven and restored to the Church. The text's answer — that a second repentance is possible, but only once — was a crucial intervention in the early Church's debate about the forgiveness of serious post-baptismal sins (murder, adultery, apostasy), and it influenced the development of the sacrament of penance in the Catholic Church. The text also provides valuable evidence for early Christian community life, prophecy, and eschatological expectation in the 2nd century CE.
